In this bonus episode to his earlier piece on AI in acoustics, Fanyu Meng introduces physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) through Ben Moseley’s widely shared blog post. Its test case, a one-dimensional damped harmonic oscillator, sits a little outside the usual acoustics fare, but a mass on a spring with friction is a close cousin of the vibrating systems acousticians deal with every day.

A conventional neural network trained on a handful of measured points can fit those points, but it is lost outside the training data: nothing tells it what physics lies behind the curve. A PINN adds a second, “physics” term to the loss function. The network is evaluated at a set of sample locations, its derivatives are computed, and the residual of the oscillator’s differential equation (mass, friction coefficient and spring stiffness) is added to the usual mean-squared error. The predictions are thereby pushed to stay consistent with the known physics, and the network reconstructs the entire oscillation from only a few data points.

Meng’s verdict: the physics-informed network trounces the naive one, but only because the physics is known in advance, and many real problems have no known model. The article closes with reader comments from Moseley’s blog and two LinkedIn threads, where practitioners point out that a simple finite-difference solver is far faster for low-dimensional problems, and that PINNs earn their keep on inverse problems, such as learning an unknown friction coefficient alongside the network weights.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “So, what is a physics-informed neural network?” by Ben Moseley, published on his blog (2021). Read the original.
